Via Lupe
Writing λύπη About

λύπη

/ˈly.pɛː/ · lu-pe

In Koine Greek, λύπη is usually translated pain, grief, or sorrow. Here it is understood as a lens, a way of looking at the world.

Via lupe: by way of grief, observing reality through the lens of grief.

Grief is not only a destination or an obstacle; it is a way of seeing. To look via lupe is to admit that grief can sharpen or blur what we perceive, and that what we notice through it deserves to be remembered, saved, and shared.

Notes on λύπη

Greek writers set λύπη against ἡδονή, pleasure or delight. It could name bodily pain, from hunger or cold or sickness, and also the sorrow of misfortune and death, or the sting of insult.

The Theological Dictionary of the New Testament notes that joy and sorrow are woven through the whole of human life, and that even the happiest things, marriage and children, bring their share of grief. It puts it plainly: there is no ἡδονή without λύπη. Sorrow, too, raises the question of why, and in doing so opens the world to us.

In the New Testament the word carries that same double edge. Paul writes that godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10), and Jesus promises his friends that your grief will turn into joy (John 16:20).

See Theological Dictionary of the New Testament, s.v. λύπη.
